patient.name: Marcus Chen
patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent severe episodic abdominal pain with progressive neuropathy and psychiatric symptoms over 18 months
patient.hpi: Marcus Chen is a 35-year-old junior attorney presenting for neurological evaluation after 18 months of recurrent severe episodic abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and intermittent psychiatric symptoms. His illness began with 3 episodes of severe colicky diffuse abdominal pain lasting 2-5 days each (first 12 months), requiring emergency room visits; imaging (CT abdomen) was consistently normal and he was told to follow up with gastroenterology. He was worked up for appendicitis, bowel obstruction, and renal colic — all negative. Gastroenterology attributed the pain to 'functional abdominal pain' or irritable bowel syndrome, but he strongly disputes this given the severity. Three months ago, he developed progressive bilateral leg weakness and sensory loss, and one month ago experienced a transient 3-day episode of confusion and disorientation (resolved spontaneously). He reports that the neuropathy episodes seem temporally related to the abdominal pain crises. He was on no psychiatric medications but was seen by psychiatry who documented 'unclear anxiety disorder with somatization' after his first confusion episode. He has noted dark discoloration of his urine during the abdominal episodes ('like port wine'). He is an attorney and has been under significant stress, attributed by multiple physicians as the cause. He takes no medications, does not drink alcohol, does not use illicit drugs, and has no relevant family history — though his maternal cousin had 'some rare blood disorder that caused seizures' (details unknown). He has not been exposed to toxins. He fasted extensively (24-hour fasts, 2-3x/month as part of an intermittent fasting regimen that he has maintained for 2 years).
pmh: Recurrent unexplained severe abdominal pain (3 ER visits, all negative imaging)

Negative: rash, fever, joint pain, weight loss.

report.summary: SEVERELY ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. PREDOMINANTLY MOTOR AXONAL NEUROPATHY — characteristic of porphyric neuropathy. In acute intermittent porphyria, neuropathy is PROXIMAL > DISTAL and MOTOR > SENSORY (different from typical diabetic/CIDP which are distal and sensorimotor). Upper motor neuron signs may also be present. EMG shows acute denervation in proximal muscles.

motor.flag: SEVERELY REDUCED AMPLITUDE — axonal motor loss; velocity mildly slow secondary to severe axonal loss
mildly reduced amplitude — motor amplitude loss relative to normal velocity

sensory.flag: mildly reduced amplitude — sensory relatively preserved compared to motor (characteristic of AIP neuropathy)

muscles_tested.spontaneous: 3+ fibrillations, 3+ PSW — SEVERE ACUTE DENERVATION IN PROXIMAL MUSCLE
muscles_tested.morphology: acute denervation (insufficient time for reinnervation — acute crisis)

emg.summary: ACUTE PREDOMINANTLY MOTOR AXONAL NEUROPATHY WITH PROXIMAL > DISTAL INVOLVEMENT — classic porphyric neuropathy. Severe acute denervation in proximal muscles (deltoid, biceps, vastus lateralis) in addition to distal muscles. Sensory NCS relatively preserved compared to motor. This pattern is DISTINCT from diabetic (distal > proximal, sensorimotor symmetric) or CIDP (demyelinating, sensorimotor).

report.overall_impression: PORPHYRIC NEUROPATHY — acute axonal motor-predominant with proximal > distal pattern. Consistent with acute intermittent porphyria. URGENT TREATMENT: IV hemin (Panhematin) 4 mg/kg/day x 4-7 days + IV glucose (10% dextrose) + correct hyponatremia. AVOID ALL UNSAFE DRUGS — many common anesthetics, anticonvulsants, antibiotics, hormones, and pain medications are porphyrinogenic.

results.citation: European Porphyria Network EPNET Drug Database 2024 (drugs-porphyria.eu)
results.summary: UNSAFE drugs in acute porphyria (partial list): Barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate (anticonvulsants — almost all are unsafe), alcohol, oral contraceptives, progesterone, sulfonamides, rifampin, griseofulvin, trimethoprim, ergots, ketamine. SAFE analgesics for porphyric pain: morphine, fentanyl, opioids (safe), acetaminophen (safe), NSAIDs (generally safe). Gabapentin is generally considered safe. Benzodiazepines are SAFE (important for agitation/seizure management). Beta-blockers are SAFE (heart rate/BP management in autonomic crisis).

output.interpretation: CRITICAL DRUG SAFETY: Anticonvulsants (especially phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, barbiturates) are PORPHYRINOGENIC and MUST NOT be used for seizure management in AIP. Safe seizure management: levetiracetam, gabapentin (preferred), benzodiazepines. For pain: opioids and acetaminophen are safe. Oral contraceptives are a major precipitant — must not be used. Hormonal IUD (progesterone) is also porphyrinogenic. Patient must carry an emergency medical ID and porphyria emergency protocol card.

results.citation: Balwani M et al. (2020) Phase 3 trial of RNAi therapeutic givosiran for acute intermittent porphyria. NEJM 382:2289-2301.
results.summary: Givosiran (siRNA targeting hepatic ALAS1 mRNA) reduces AIP attack rate by 74% vs placebo. SC injection monthly. FDA-approved for recurrent AIP attacks. Normalizes urinary ALA/PBG in most patients. Side effects: injection site reactions, nausea, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs). Improves neuropathy outcomes by preventing recurrent porphyric neurological crises.

output.interpretation: Givosiran is indicated for this patient given: recurrent attacks (3 severe abdominal crises), peripheral neuropathy (indicates severe disease), transient encephalopathy episode. Monthly SC injection. Monitor LFTs. Expected to reduce attack frequency by 74% and prevent further neuropathy progression. Combined with strict avoidance of precipitants (fasting, porphyrinogenic drugs).

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) with porphyric neuropathy — HMBS pathogenic variant c.518G>A
critical_actions: Order urine PBG DURING a symptomatic episode — collecting during remission may miss the diagnosis
IV hemin URGENTLY — hemin suppresses ALAS1, reducing porphyrin precursor accumulation

STRICT DRUG SAFETY: Avoid all porphyrinogenic drugs — the safe drug list must be printed and given to patient; anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate) are UNSAFE if seizure management is needed; use levetiracetam/benzodiazepines
STOP FASTING REGIMEN — caloric restriction is a major precipitant; patient must NOT fast
Genetic counseling for family — autosomal dominant condition; sister is a carrier
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT attribute to IBS or anxiety — elevated PBG is objective; psychiatric misattribution in AIP can be fatal if attack progresses to respiratory failure
Do NOT use phenytoin, carbamazepine, or valproate for seizure management in AIP — these are PORPHYRINOGENIC and will worsen the attack
Do NOT prescribe oral contraceptives or hormonal therapy — porphyrinogenic
Do NOT allow patient to continue intermittent fasting — carbohydrate restriction directly triggers ALAS1 upregulation and AIP attacks

differential.key_distinguishing: IBS does not cause peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy, port-wine urine, hyponatremia, or tachycardia; recurrent severe colicky pain requiring ER visits is NOT IBS pattern; PBG 42 mmol/mol is objective
Elevated urine PBG and ALA are objective biochemical findings; hyponatremia and tachycardia are not somatoform; psychiatric misattribution is one of the most dangerous errors in AIP
Heavy metals screen normal; arsenic/lead can cause abdominal pain + neuropathy but do not cause port-wine urine or elevated PBG
CIDP is not episodic with abdominal crisis; CIDP is demyelinating on NCS; CIDP does not cause port-wine urine, hyponatremia, or elevated porphyrins

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three levels of misdirection — (1) 3 normal abdominal CT scans labeled as functional, (2) psychiatric symptoms labeled as anxiety/somatization, (3) neuropathy worked up without considering AIP
KEY CLUE: PORT-WINE URINE during attacks is pathognomonic — must ALWAYS check urine color during attacks and test PBG immediately

FASTING PRECIPITANT: Patient's self-prescribed 24-hour intermittent fasting 2-3x/month was directly triggering attacks for 2 years — carbohydrate restriction is one of the most potent AIP precipitants
NCS PATTERN: Predominantly MOTOR axonal with PROXIMAL > DISTAL = porphyric neuropathy (distinct from diabetic distal sensorimotor, CIDP demyelinating, or axonal length-dependent patterns)
HYPONATREMIA IN AIP: SIADH from hypothalamic involvement — a unique metabolic clue not present in other neuropathy causes
DRUG SAFETY: AIP drug list is critically important — many common hospital medications are unsafe; patients must carry an emergency drug list
AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT: 50% risk to siblings and children; maternal cousin's 'seizures and blood disorder' were unrecognized AIP attacks
